title: Day 6: Real Oscillations (Eventually)
text:
The day started away from the code. Day 5 had left a few conceptual gaps, specifically around what it actually means for a system to oscillate versus ring transiently and so I spent the morning working through the nonlinear dynamics textbook (Strogatz) rather than jumping back into R straight away.
The focus was on two areas. First, phase portraits in 2D, the geometry of how trajectories move through the \((x, \dot{x})\) plane, what nullclines are and how they carve up the phase plane, and how to read off qualitative behaviour (stable nodes, spirals, saddle points) from the portrait without solving the equations explicitly. Being comfortable reading a phase portrait is basically a prerequisite for understanding any of the oscillation dynamics in the mizer model.
Second, the existence and uniqueness theorem which is the result that guarantees a unique solution through every initial condition, given the function f is continuously differentiable . This matters for simulations more than it might seem: if you’re running a numerical integrator and getting different trajectories depending on step size, it’s worth knowing whether that’s a numerical error or a sign that the theorem’s conditions actually break down somewhere in parameter space.

title: Day 6: Real Oscillations (Eventually)
text:
The Uncomfortable Check
My supervisor pointed out something I’d missed: the oscillations from Day 5 could be integration artefacts. The obvious test is to switch to a more accurate integration method and see if the feature survives.
Mizer supports a predictor-corrector integration method alongside the default. The predictor-corrector is second-order and has better error properties than the default scheme, if oscillations are real dynamics rather than integration artefacts, they should persist regardless of which method you use. Swapping in method = "predictor-corrector" is a one-line change:
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| output: false

sim <- project(params, t_max = 100, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
The oscillations disappeared, the biomass converged smoothly to equilibrium instead. That’s a clear sign: what I’d been looking at was a discretisation error, not a genuine feature of the model’s dynamics. The default integrator was producing numerical ringing that mimicked real oscillations.
Not a great feeling, but better to find out now. The dynamics aren’t as interesting as I thought, or at least, not under these parameter settings.

title: Day 6: Real Oscillations (Eventually)
text:
A Pointer from the Literature
With the original oscillations ruled out, the question became: is there a parameter regime where mizer does produce genuine cycles? I was almost certain the answer should be yes, the biological mechanisms for a Hopf bifurcation are clearly present in a size-structured consumer-resource model but I didn’t know where in parameter space to look.
At this point I was reminded of a piece of code I’d come across earlier in the project: a worked example on RPubs showing plankton-anchovy oscillations in mizer.
https://rpubs.com/gustav/plankton-anchovy
Reading through it, the setup was different from what I’d been doing, a two-species model (anchovy feeding on plankton) with specific parameter choices that had been tuned to produce interesting dynamics. The code was written for an older version of mizer, so several of the functions had changed names or signatures.
I worked through it and translated the setup to current mizer, newSingleSpeciesParams() in place of the old direct constructor, setResource() for the resource dynamics, and resource_semichemostat as the dynamics type. The key parameters from the original that produced oscillations were a low resource replenishment rate combined with a large predator-prey size ratio exactly the instability regime from Datta, Delius & Law (2011).


Code
library(mizer)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
p <- list(
  dt     = 0.001,
  dx     = 0.1,
  w_min  = 0.0003,
  w_max  = 66.5,
  w_mat  = 10,
  alpha  = 0.1,      # assimilation efficiency
  gamma  = 750,
  lambda = 2,
  a0     = 100
)

kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
  species_name = "Anchovy",
  w_min  = p$w_min,
  w_max  = p$w_max,
  w_mat  = p$w_mat,
  no_w   = no_w,
  lambda = p$lambda,
  kappa  = kappa,
  alpha  = p$alpha,
  gamma  = p$gamma,
  ks     = 0
)

r <- resource_rate(params)
r <- r * 0.001
params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r,
                      resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")


The r * 0.001 scaling is the critical detail, suppressing plankton replenishment to roughly a thousandth of its default value is what puts the system in the oscillatory regime.

title: Day 6: Real Oscillations (Eventually)
text:
The Oscillations That Survive
Running the adapted model with the predictor-corrector method, and introducing a perturbation mid-run by crashing the large size class to a thousandth of its current abundance:


Code
test_sizes <- list(
  "small"  = c(0.1, 1),
  "medium" = c(1, 10),
  "large"  = c(10, 100)
)

params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1
T1 <- 10

sim <- project(params, t_max = T1, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

rng <- test_sizes[["large"]]
idx <- params@w >= rng[1] & params@w <= rng[2]
last <- dim(sim@n)[1]
sim@n[last, , idx] <- sim@n[last, , idx] / 10^3

sim <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
               progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
# can also use tr_bdf2, but needs much finer dt


The animated size spectrum gives the first read on whether anything interesting is happening:


Code
nf        <- melt(sim@n)
names(nf) <- c("time", "sp", "w", "value")

n_ppf        <- melt(sim@n_pp)
names(n_ppf) <- c("time", "w", "value")
n_ppf$sp     <- "Plankton"

nf <- rbind(nf, n_ppf)

nf_plot <- nf %>%
  filter(w > 10^-5, time >= 50) %>%
  mutate(b = value * w^2)

plot_ly(nf_plot) %>%
  add_lines(
    x = ~w, y = ~b,
    color = ~sp,
    frame = ~time,
    line = list(simplify = FALSE)
  ) %>%
  layout(
    xaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                 title_text = "body mass (g)"),
    yaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                 title_text = "biomass (g/m^3)",
                 range = c(-8, 0))
  )


Warning in registerFrames(p, frameMapping = frameMapping): NaNs produced






The oscillations were still there. Switching to a more accurate method didn’t make them disappear, the exact opposite of what happened with the old parameter set. If the oscillations survive a change in integration method, they’re real. These are genuine limit cycle dynamics, not the numerical noise previously.

title: Day 6: Real Oscillations (Eventually)
text:
What Period?
With a credible oscillation in hand, the next question was what sets its period. The first tool was a biomass time series broken down by component, total Anchovy, “small Anchovy” (0.01–0.4 g), and Plankton, which makes the phase relationships visible:


Code
abm  <- melt(getBiomass(sim))
abmr <- melt(getBiomass(sim, min_w = 0.01, max_w = 0.4))
abmr$sp <- "small Anchovy"

pbm <- sim@n_pp %*% (params@w_full * params@dw_full)
pbm <- melt(pbm)
names(pbm)[names(pbm) == "Var1"] <- "time"
pbm$Var2 <- NULL
pbm$sp <- "Plankton"

bm <- rbind(pbm, abm, abmr)

bm_plot <- bm %>% filter(time >= 10)

plot_ly(bm_plot) %>%
  add_lines(x = ~time, y = ~value, color = ~sp) %>%
  layout(
    yaxis = list(type = "log", exponentformat = "power",
                 title_text = "biomass (g/m^3)",
                 range = c(-7, 2)),
    xaxis = list(title_text = "time (year)")
  )






The three-component plot is more informative than total Anchovy alone, “small Anchovy” tracks the recruitment pulse, which leads the adult biomass signal by part of a generation. Eyeballing the period from this plot, the oscillations looked to be somewhere around 3–3.5 years.
Settling on that range, the natural question is: what in the biology sets this timescale?

Two Generations
The obvious candidate is generation time, the time for a recruit to grow from minimum size to maturity. If the consumer-resource feedback loop runs on a delay equal to the time fish take to grow up and start reproducing, the oscillation period should be some multiple of that delay.


Code
gc <- getGrowthCurves(sim, species = "Anchovy", max_age = 20)
age <- as.numeric(colnames(gc))
w_of_age <- gc["Anchovy", ]

age_at_mat <- approx(x = w_of_age, y = age, xout = p$w_mat, rule = 2)$y
age_at_mat


[1] 2.636306


Code
# [1] ~1.6 years


A single generation is around 1.6 years. Two generations is roughly 3.2 years which is very close to the observed oscillation period.
This makes biological sense as a mechanism. A pulse of recruits grows up, reaches maturity, and exerts grazing pressure on the resource. The resource dips in response. The reduced food slows growth for the next cohort, delaying its own maturation. By the time that cohort reaches full reproductive output, the resource has had time to recover and the cycle repeats. The characteristic delay in this feedback is two maturation transit times, not one, because it takes one generation for the signal (resource depletion) to translate into the response (delayed next cohort), and another generation for that response to feed back into the resource again.
It’s not a precise derivation, but it’s the right order of magnitude and the right mechanism.

title: Day 6: Real Oscillations (Eventually)
text:
What’s Next

Verify the period more carefully: the peak-finding approach is sensitive to how much of the transient you include. Worth repeating with just the settled part of the time series (say, t > 100) and comparing to the ACF result.
Link the period to parameters explicitly: If the period is set by maturation time, varying w_mat or growth rate parameters should shift the period predictably. This is a testable prediction and would make the mechanism much more concrete.
Connect back to the original project question: the plankton-anchovy model from RPubs is a two-species example, but the project is ultimately about single-species dynamics and whether fishing can relieve size-spectrum jams. Now that there’s a confirmed limit cycle in hand, the next step is understanding whether the same dynamics can be produced in a single-species setup and if so, under what parameters.

Today involved more backtracking than I’d have liked, but ruling out the discretisation artefacts was necessary work. The oscillations in the RPubs example are the real thing, and they’re now a concrete starting point rather than a vague hope.

title: Day 4: Finding the Stability Boundary
text:
Finding Oscillations
The starting point was confirming that the oscillatory behaviour found yesterday wasn’t a one-off. By systematically varying \(\sigma\) (diet breadth) across a range of values while keeping \(\beta\) fixed, it was possible to see clearly that oscillation amplitude increases as \(\sigma\) decreases: smaller diet breadth means tighter predator-prey coupling, which amplifies perturbations rather than absorbing them.
The key to making this comparison meaningful was measuring relative amplitude, the peak-to-peak oscillation as a fraction of the mean biomass, rather than absolute amplitude. Absolute amplitude is confounded by the steady-state biomass level, which itself changes with \(\sigma\) and \(\beta\). Relative amplitude strips that out and gives a like-for-like comparison across parameter combinations.






NoteAn example of the oscillations( \(\beta\) = 30, \(\sigma\) = 0.5)




library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse) 
library(glue)


# Deviation from power law
deviation_plot <- function(sim, title) {
  spec <- finalNResource(sim)
  expected <- params@w_full^(-2.05)
  deviation <- spec / expected
  plot(params@w_full, deviation, type = "l", log = "x",
       main = title, xlab = "Size (g)", ylab = "Deviation from power law")
  abline(h = 1, lty = 2)
}

test_sizes <- list(
  "small"  = c(0.1, 1),
  "medium" = c(1, 10),
  "large"  = c(10, 100)
)#size ranges in which we are changing the initial population
par(mfrow = c(5, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))  # 3 rows (one per size range), 1 columns (deviation)

varying_beta_sigma_test <- function(beta_new = 100, sigma_new = 1.3) {
  test_sizes <- list(
    "small"  = c(0.1, 1),
    "medium" = c(1, 10),
    "large"  = c(10, 100)
  )
  par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  p <- newSingleSpeciesParams(lambda = 2.05, beta = beta_new, sigma = sigma_new)
  
  r <- resource_rate(p)
  r <- r * 0.001
  p <- setResource(p, resource_rate = r, resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  rng <- test_sizes[["large"]]
  idx <- p@w >= rng[1] & p@w <= rng[2]
  initialN(p)[, idx] <- initialN(p)[, idx] * 5
  
  sim <- project(p, t_max = 100, t_save = 0.5)
  animateSpectra(sim, resource = FALSE, log_x = FALSE, log_y = FALSE, power = 2)
}


varying_beta_sigma_test(beta_new = 30,sigma_new=0.5)

title: Day 4: Finding the Stability Boundary
text:
Mapping the Phase Diagram
The main result of the day was a phase diagram of oscillation amplitude across a grid of \((\beta, \sigma)\) values. For each combination, a simulation was run and the relative amplitude computed over the final 10 time units, late enough that transient startup effects have died away, but still capturing any sustained oscillations.

library(mizer)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse)

varying_beta_sigma <- function(beta_new, sigma_new) {
  p <- newSingleSpeciesParams(lambda = 2.05, beta = beta_new, sigma = sigma_new)
  r <- resource_rate(p)
  r <- r * 0.001
  p <- setResource(p, resource_rate = r, resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  idx <- p@w >= 10 & p@w <= 100
  initialN(p)[, idx] <- initialN(p)[, idx] * 5
  project(p, t_max = 100, t_save = 0.5)
}

amplitude_finder <- function(t_max, sims) {
  times    <- as.numeric(dimnames(sims@n)[[1]])
  time_idx <- times >= t_max - 10 & times <= t_max
  n_sub    <- sims@n[time_idx, , , drop = FALSE]
  list(
    n_max = apply(n_sub, 3, max) * sims@params@w^2,
    n_min = apply(n_sub, 3, min) * sims@params@w^2
  )
}

max_amplitude <- function(sim) {
  res    <- amplitude_finder(t_max = 100, sims = sim)
  n_mean <- (res$n_max + res$n_min) / 2
  max((res$n_max - res$n_min) / n_mean, na.rm = TRUE)
}

beta_values  <- c(10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200, 500)
sigma_values <- c(0.3, 0.5,0.6,0.7, 0.8, 1.0, 1.3, 1.5)

phase_grid <- expand.grid(beta = beta_values, sigma = sigma_values)
phase_grid$amplitude <- mapply(function(b, s) {
  sim <- varying_beta_sigma(beta_new = b, sigma_new = s)
  max_amplitude(sim)
}, phase_grid$beta, phase_grid$sigma)


ggplot(phase_grid, aes(x = beta, y = sigma, z = amplitude)) +
  geom_contour_filled() +
  geom_point(aes(colour = amplitude), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = expression(beta), y = expression(sigma),
       fill = "Relative amplitude",
       title = "Phase diagram: oscillation amplitude") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Day 4: Finding the Stability Boundary
text:
What the Phase Diagram Shows
The result is striking. A few things stand out immediately:
\(\sigma\) is the dominant parameter. The contour lines run roughly horizontally, meaning the amplitude is much more sensitive to diet breadth than to predator-to-prey size ratio. Above \(\sigma \approx 0.8\), the system is stable across all values of \(\beta\) tested and the spectrum settles to steady state regardless of the perturbation.
Below \(\sigma \approx 0.5\), oscillations become large. In this regime the relative amplitude approaches 2.0, meaning the peak biomass is roughly three times the trough. These are not subtle fluctuations but sustained swings in the size spectrum.
\(\beta\) plays a secondary role. Smaller \(\beta\) slightly amplifies the oscillations, but it doesn’t drive them on its own.
The stability boundary sits around \(\sigma \approx 0.6\)–\(0.8\), with a slight dependence on \(\beta\). This is the parameter regime worth probing more carefully as it’s where the transition from stable to oscillatory dynamics occurs.
One caveat: the contour plot interpolates between a grid of simulation points. Some of the finer features could be interpolation artefacts. A denser grid would give more trustworthy contours,but would take a long time to render.

title: Day 4: Finding the Stability Boundary
text:
What’s Next
Today produced a clear map of the parameter space, but it also raised questions that need a stronger theoretical foundation to answer properly.
Read more papers: The phase diagram raises specific questions like why does \(\sigma\) dominate over \(\beta\)? What governs the shape of the stability boundary? Is the elbow real? These are questions the literature on size spectrum instability and bifurcation theory should be able to speak to. The next step is to go back to the papers, particularly Datta et al. and Rochet & Benoît, and read them with these specific questions in mind.
Build up knowledge of bifurcations and nonlinear dynamics: The stability boundary found today is, in the language of dynamical systems, a bifurcation curve, the line in parameter space where the system transitions from a stable fixed point to a limit cycle. Understanding that transition properly (what type of bifurcation it is, whether it’s subcritical or supercritical, what that implies for the system’s response to perturbations) requires working through the relevant nonlinear dynamics. That groundwork will make the next round of simulations much more targeted.
The pieces are starting to come together. The stability boundary exists, it’s visible, and now it needs to be understood.

title: Day Two: Git, GitHub & Mizer Traffic Jams
text: Yesterday ended with a plan: get MIZER running, build the simplest possible single-species model, and try to see a jam. Simple enough on paper. What I didn’t account for was that before any of that, the project needed to actually be on GitHub and setting up Git inside RStudio turned out to be its own battle entirely.

title: Day Two: Git, GitHub & Mizer Traffic Jams
text:
The Git Problem
I’ve used Git before, but always through VS Code on WSL. The workflow there is second nature: open a terminal, git init, git add, git commit, done. RStudio’s Git panel is a completely different mental model, and for a while it wasn’t obvious where anything lived or why it wasn’t behaving.
The first surprise was the line ending warnings. Every file I staged threw a wall of:
warning: LF will be replaced by CRLF the next time Git touches it
On WSL this never comes up because you’re already on a Linux filesystem. On native Windows, Git is converting line endings between the repo and the working directory, and RStudio doesn’t hide that from you. It’s not an error, just noise but it took a while to confirm that, because my instinct was that something had gone wrong. The fix was a .gitattributes file telling Git to handle line endings consistently and stop warning about it.
The second problem was worse. Trying to push anything longer than a short path failed silently at first, and then failed loudly with a cryptic error about the path being too long. Windows caps file paths at 260 characters by default, and the project folder name alone is already a good chunk of that. The fix is a single config flag:
git config --global core.longpaths true
But it also requires enabling long paths at the Windows level via the registry, which isn’t something I’d ever had to think about on WSL.
The third thing (this one stalled me for a good twenty minutes) was credentials. RStudio asked for a GitHub password and rejected it, because GitHub stopped accepting passwords in 2021. You need a Personal Access Token. Once I generated one and pointed Git at the Windows Credential Manager with git config --global credential.helper manager, everything went through cleanly. But it wasn’t obvious that was the issue until I dug into the error message properly.
By the end of it the repo was on GitHub and rendering to GitHub Pages via the docs/ folder. That felt like a real win, but it had taken most of the morning.

title: Day Two: Git, GitHub & Mizer Traffic Jams
text:
Getting into Mizer
With the repo sorted, the afternoon was for MIZER.Initially, I ran into a problem,which was that I had accidentally installed an older version of Mizer,without any of the newer functions. Updating it was straightforward enough, devtools::install_github("sizespectrum/mizer"), though it requires Rtools on Windows since it compiles from source, which added another fifteen minutes of waiting.
The first model came together quickly. A single species, a resource spectrum, default parameters:

library(mizer)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse)
params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(lambda = 2.05)
sim_base <- project(params, t_max = 100)
plotSpectra(sim_base, time_range = 90:100)








And it worked. The spectrum was there, smooth, exactly what you’d expect; a clean power law line on a log-log plot. Which was the problem.

title: Day Two: Git, GitHub & Mizer Traffic Jams
text:
Breaking the Steady State
This is where the day got frustrating.
MIZER’s project() function runs the model forward in time and stores snapshots at each timestep. The idea was to animate those snapshots and watch the spectrum evolve, to see whether a jam would nucleate and grow. But when I tried to build the animation, nothing moved. The model reached its steady state so quickly that by t = 10 or so, all 100 frames of the animation were essentially identical. You’d press play and nothing would happen.
The problem is that newSingleSpeciesParams() initialises the model at a state that’s already close to equilibrium. The dynamics exist, the model can move, but it has nowhere to go because it starts near the fixed point. It’s like trying to film a pendulum by starting it in the vertical position.
The solution, once I found it, was obvious in retrospect. You have to start the model somewhere far from steady state so it has to travel to get there:

# Resource rate experiments
params_low_r <- setResource(params, resource_rate = 0.001, resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")

initialN(params) <- initialN(params) * 0.01
initialN(params_low_r) <- initialN(params_low_r) * 0.01

# Baseline
sim_base <- project(params, t_max = 100)

# Low resource rate
sim_low_r <- project(params_low_r, t_max = 100)

Knocking the fish population down to 1% of their equilibrium values forces the whole system to rebuild from scratch. Now when you animate it, you can actually watch the spectrum grow and settle and more importantly, you can see whether it settles smoothly or whether a bump forms along the way.






NoteMaking the animation



Making the simulation was much simpler than I first thought, mainly thanks to the new functions.

animateSpectra(sim_low_r)







The other diagnostic was the deviation from power law plot, applied to the resource spectrum.






NoteDeviation from Power Law Plot



This plot divides the actual resource spectrum by the expected power law at each size class. The baseline should sit at a constant ratio across all sizes. Any departure from that flat line means the resource is accumulating or being depleted at that size relative to what the power law predicts.

deviation_plot <- function(sim, title) {
  spec <- finalNResource(sim)
  expected <- params@w_full^(-2.05)
  deviation <- spec / expected
  plot(params@w_full, deviation, type = "l", log = "x",
       main = title, xlab = "Size (g)", ylab = "Deviation from power law")
  abline(h = 1, lty = 2)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
deviation_plot(sim_base,  "Baseline")
deviation_plot(sim_low_r, "Low resource rate")

title: Day Two: Git, GitHub & Mizer Traffic Jams
text:
What the Experiments Showed
With the animation working, I ran two variants: baseline and low resource replenishment (resource_rate = 0.001). The deviation-from-power-law plot on the resource spectrum made the contrast between the two cases visible.
The baseline was a flat line. The resource sits at a constant ratio to the power law across every size class, which is exactly what you would expect from a system at steady state. The low resource rate case was different: a small positive bump appeared at very small plankton sizes, and a clear dip appeared at around 1g, precisely where the fish feed most actively. When replenishment is slow, fish draw the resource down faster than it can recover at that size, and the deficit shows up cleanly in the plot.
That is a proof of mechanism rather than a positive result. The model is behaving correctly and the physics is there, but the resource depletion at 0.001 is only about 0.2% below the power law baseline. That is not deep enough to meaningfully slow fish growth or cause biomass to pile up at that size. The maturation bottleneck is still dominating the signal completely. To see a resource-driven jam, the replenishment rate needs to be pushed much lower, to the point where the depletion at feeding size actually forces fish to slow down and accumulate.

title: Day Two: Git, GitHub & Mizer Traffic Jams
text:
What Tomorrow Looks Like
The steady-state issue is solved, the animation works, and the baseline experiments are done. Next is to try to push the model into the regime where resource dynamics, rather than maturation, are the dominant source of instability. That probably means:

Much lower values of resource_rate than I tried today
Trying a multi-species model where a predator depends tightly on prey, so the predator-prey feedback can create its own oscillations
Starting to think about what a proper bifurcation diagram would look like, sweeping across one parameter and recording where the spectrum deviates from the power law
Increasing or decreasing the starting population in a specific range

The goal is still intuition-building, not results. But I want to at least see a resource-driven instability before I start trying to characterise it.

title: Day Two: Git, GitHub & Mizer Traffic Jams
text:
Reflection
Today was a day of friction. The Git problems in the morning weren’t intellectually interesting, they were just obstacles, the kind of thing that costs time without teaching you anything useful about the actual project. But they’re sorted now, the repo is live, and that won’t have to be done again.
The Mizer work was more rewarding, even where it was frustrating. The steady-state problem felt like a dead end for a while, but the fix made me think harder about what the model is actually doing and the realisation that MIZER initialises near equilibrium by design is genuinely useful context for everything that follows. You can’t just run the model and hope for dynamics, you have to consciously choose your initial conditions.
On to the next parameter sweep.

title: Stuff that’s confusing
text:
Here is the code that produced the confusing result:

library(mizer)
library(patchwork)

title: Stuff that’s confusing
text:
What plotSpectraRelative Actually Computes
The function takes two simulations and plots, at each size class \(w\):
\[\text{relative difference}(w) = \frac{N_2(w) - N_1(w)}{N_1(w)}\]
where \(N_1\) is the final spectrum from the first argument and \(N_2\) is the final spectrum from the second argument. It does this separately for the resource spectrum and for each fish species.
So plotSpectraRelative(sim_base_no_reduction, sim_low_r) is answering the question:

At the end of the run, how does sim_low_r differ from sim_base_no_reduction, as a fraction of s im_base_no_reduction?

That sounds reasonable. The problem is in what actually differs between those two simulations.

title: Stuff that’s confusing
section: Why the Dipole Shape Is Confusing
text:
Why the Dipole Shape Is Confusing
The resource line shows a sharp negative dip at roughly 1–10g followed by an equally sharp positi ve spike at roughly 10–100g. This , a jam precursor, or some structured oscillation. It is probably none of those things.
In single-species MIZER, fish feed on prey roughly \(1/\beta\) of their own body mass, where \(\beta \appr
ox 100\) by default. A fish of mass 100g–1000g feeds on resource in the range 1g–10g. So:

The dip at 1–10g is the feeding zone: lower resource rate means slower replenishment, so fish dra w the resource down more at those sizes. That part is real and is a resource-rate effect.
The spike at 10–100g is harder to read. These are sizes at the upper end of the resource spectrum , above where the fish feed most actively. The excess there likely reflects a transient: sim_low_r st arted with very few fish, so during less grazing pressure at those sizes, and by \(t = 100\) the resource may not yet be fully equilibrated at the top end of its spectrum.

In other words: the dipole is a mixtfect (the dip) and a residual transien t (the spike) that exists because sim_low_r started from a completely different initial condition.

The Target species line is essentially zero across all sizes. This means both simulations produced near ly identical fish spectra by \(t = 100\), despite starting at different initial populations and having di fferent resource rates.
This is actually a useful diagnostic result, but not a reassuring one. It says one of two things:

The fish dynamics equilibrate fast enough that both runs converged to the same fish steady state by \(t = 100\) regardless of where they started. In that case, the fish spectrum is not sensitive to resourc e rate at this parameter regime, which reinforces the Day Two finding that the maturation bottleneck is dominating.
The fish in sim_low_r are still recovering from the 1% knockdown, but their recovery trajectory ha ppened to land at almost the same fish density as sim_base_no_reduction at \(t = 100\) by coincidence o f timing.

Either way, the flat fish line is not evidence that the resource rate doesn’t matter — it is evidence that the fish converge to approximately the same abundance regardless, which means the system is not i n the instability regime yet.

text:
Nagel & Schreckenberg (1992) — A Cellular Automaton Model for Freeway Traffic Journal de Physique I, 2, 2221–2229 https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1992JPhy1…2.2221N The original discrete traffic model. Monte Carlo simulations show a sharp phase transition from free flow to stop-and-go jams as vehicle density crosses a critical threshold — the clearest demonstration that jamming is a collective, density-driven phenomenon, not caused by a bottleneck.



Bando, Hasebe, Nakayama, Shibata & Sugiyama (1995) — Dynamical Model of Traffic Congestion and Numerical Simulation Physical Review E, 51, 1035–1042 https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.51.1035 Introduces the Optimal Velocity (OV) model, a microscopic car-following model. Stability analysis reveals a Hopf bifurcation at a critical density: below it, uniform flow is stable; above it, small perturbations grow into oscillatory stop-and-go waves. The bifurcation parameter maps cleanly onto the fish growth-rate sensitivity. ***
Kerner & Konhäuser (1994) — Structure and Parameters of Clusters in Traffic Flow Physical Review E, 50(1), 54–83 https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.50.54 Studies the nonlinear structure of jams (clusters) once they form. Derives explicit formulas for the density, velocity, and propagation speed inside and outside a jam as functions of the background density — i.e. the constants that characterise whether a jam will form and what it will look like.



Richards (1956) — Shock Waves on the Highway Operations Research, 4(1), 42–51 https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.4.1.42 The third paper in the LWR trio (with Lighthill & Whitham 1955). Shows that the conservation PDE develops shock waves — sharp discontinuities in density — precisely when the flux-density curve is concave. The condition for shock formation is the direct traffic analogue of the jamming instability criterion in the fish model. ***
Flynn, Kasimov, Nave, Rosales & Seibold (2009) — Self-Sustained Nonlinear Waves in Traffic Flow Physical Review E, 79, 056113 https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.79.056113 Proves analytically that the Payne–Whitham second-order traffic model admits jamitons — self-sustaining nonlinear traveling waves analogous to detonation waves in combustion. Derives existence conditions and wave speed from first principles. The closest mathematical paper to the fish “pile-up” wave the project is trying to find.



Seibold, Flynn, Kasimov & Rosales (2013) — Constructing Set-Valued Fundamental Diagrams from Jamiton Solutions Networks and Heterogeneous Media, 8(3), 745–772 https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.2828 Shows how the multi-valued (unstable) region of the fundamental diagram — the flow-density curve — arises directly from jamiton solutions. The set-valued region is exactly the regime where jams spontaneously form, giving a precise mathematical characterisation of the unstable parameter space. ***
Sugiyama et al. (2008) — Traffic Jams Without Bottlenecks: Experimental Evidence New Journal of Physics, 10, 033001 https://doi.org/10.1088/1367-2630/10/3/033001 The landmark ring-road experiment: 22 cars drive in a circle and, without any obstruction, a jam emerges spontaneously above a critical density of 22 vehicles. Provides empirical confirmation that the Hopf bifurcation predicted by OV models is real. This is the traffic equivalent of what the MIZER simulations are trying to demonstrate for fish.



Colombo (2002) — Hyperbolic Phase Transitions in Traffic Flow SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics, 63, 708–721 https://doi.org/10.1137/S0036139901393184 Formulates traffic as a system with two distinct phases — free flow (scalar conservation law) and congested flow (2×2 system) — coupled at a free boundary. The phase transition is mathematically sharp and rigorously solved. Directly relevant to understanding the fish model’s transition between “smooth spectrum” and “jammed” states. ***
Bifurcation Analysis of Macroscopic Traffic Flow Models Based on Driver Behavior (2023)* ResearchGate preprint / journal https://www.researchgate.net/publication/376606973_Bifurcation_analysis_of_macroscopic_traffic_flow_models_based_on_driver_behavior A more recent paper that explicitly proves the existence of Hopf bifurcations and saddle-node bifurcations in macroscopic traffic flow models as sensitivity parameters vary. Directly bridges the traffic and dynamical-systems language — useful for understanding what type of instability the fish project is dealing with.



Datta, Delius & Law (2011) — A Stability Analysis of the Power-Law Steady State of Marine Size Spectra Journal of Mathematical Biology, 63(4), 779–799traffic flow models as sensitivity parameters vary. Directly bridges the traffic and dynamical-systems language — useful for understanding what type of instability the fish project is dealing with.
Sheldon, Prakash & Sutcliffe (1972) — The Size Distribution of Particles in the Ocean Limnology and Oceanography, 17(3), 327–340 https://doi.org/10.4319/lo.1972.17.3.0327 The empirical starting point for the whole field. Shows that roughly equal biomass exists at every logarithmic size class from bacteria to whales — the observation that motivated size-spectrum modelling. ***
Andersen & Beyer (2006) — Asymptotic Size Determines Species Abundance in the Marine Size Spectrum The American Naturalist, 168(1) https://doi.org/10.1086/504849 Derives, from first principles, how fish abundance scales with body mass using the predation kernel and physiology. The theoretical backbone of MIZER.



Hartvig, Andersen & Beyer (2011) — Food Webd Populations Journal of Theoretical Biology, 272(1), 113–122 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2010.12.006 The paper that defines the MIZER framework in he semi-chemostat plankton dynamics, and theMcKendrick–von Foerster PDE as used in this project. Essential reading. ***
Benoît & Rochet (2004) — A Continuous Model of Biomass Size Spectra Governed by Predation and the Effects of Fishing Journal of Theoretical Biology, 226(1) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2003.08.007 Introduces the continuous PDE model for marinerecedes MIZER, and already examines how fishing deforms the spectrum. Good for understanding where the equations come from.



Scott, Blanchard & Andersen (2014) — mizer: An R Package for Multispecies, Trait-Based and Community Size Spectrum Ecological Modelling Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 5(10) https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12256 The primary software paper for MIZER. Read this before running any simulations — it explains how the equations are discretised and which parameters control what. ***
Andersen & Pedersen (2010) — Fishing Destabilises the Biomass Flow in Marine Size Spectra Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 279(1727), 284–292 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223683/ Shows that fishing amplifies oscillations in the size spectrum, with selective fishing (targeting a narrow size range) being most destabilising. Directly relevant to the question of whether fishing can relieve jams.



Brechner et al. (2021) — Spatial Drivers of Instability in Marine Size-Spectrum Ecosystems Journal of Theoretical Biology, 516, 110631 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2021.110631 Extends size-spectrum instability into space, showing that spatial movement and fitness-taxis can produce Turing-like patterns of abundance. A natural next step oncial jamming instability. ***
Zhang & Chen (2017) — Evaluating Fishing Effects on the Stability of Fish Communities Using a Size-Spectrum Model Fisheries Research https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/ Applied study using a size-spectrum model to test how varying fishing pressure affects community stability indicators. Good for seeing how the theoretical instability plays out in a practical management context.



Lighthill & Whitham (1955) — On Kinematic ong Rivers Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 229(1178) https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1955.0112 The original paper deriving the LWR conservation PDE — the exact traffic-flow equation your supervisor used as the analogy for the fish model. Reading the source makes the mathematical parallel to the McKendrick–von Foerster equation very clear. ***

title: Day One: Setting the Stage
text:
The meeting this morning was a lot to take in. The idea that fishing could actually improve ecosystem productivity rather than harm it feels almost counterintuitive at first. But once the traffic analogy clicked, it made complete sense. Fish biomass flowing through size space behaves mathematically like cars on a motorway. When conditions are right, you get a phantom traffic jam, a pile-up at one size class that starves the fish above and below it. And just as motorway agencies can use speed limits to prevent jams, targeted fishing could in theory relieve them.
That’s the project. It’s a genuinely novel idea and it’s exciting to be working on it from day one.

title: Day One: Setting the Stage
text:
What We Got Through Today

Cleaning Up the Meeting Notes
The first thing I did was sort out the raw transcript from this morning’s meeting.
I also converted everything in the notes folder to markdown so it’s all in one consistent, readable format. The Understanding of the project.md file got a full rewrite as in my first draft, it was a wall of text before, with no structure and a couple of logical errors. Now it has proper sections, the governing equations laid out cleanly with variable tables, and a clear explanation of why low resource replenishment creates jams (which required actually thinking through the equilibrium algebra rather than just restating the supervisor’s words).


Finding Simulation Tools
Found some genuinely useful interactive simulations to build intuition with:

Martin Treiber’s ring-road sim — you can nudge one car and watch a jam propagate backward. Extremely satisfying.
MIT’s jamiton page — interactive explorable explanations of the LWR PDE, directly tied to the equations discussed in the meeting.
The MIZER interactive course — runs R in the background via Binder. This one is directly on the path to what I’ll be doing in code tomorrow.



Literature — Twenty Papers and Counting
I put together two reading lists: ten papers on the fish side and ten on the traffic side. The fish papers run from Sheldon et al.’s foundational 1972 observation that marine biomass is roughly flat across logarithmic size classes all the way through to the MIZER software paper. The traffic papers focus specifically on bifurcations, phase transitions, and the critical constants that imply jam formation.

text:
The Paper Analysis
This is where the day got genuinely hard.
Seven papers are sitting in the papers folder, and I worked through all of them in depth to produce a full analysis PDF. Some of them were dense in a way that required real concentration. Kerner & Konhäuser (1994) in particular is a 30-page Physical Review paper packed with phase-plane analysis, nonlinear cluster theory, and pages of coupled ODEs. These are not light reads.
But the key is that they’re all saying versions of the same thing, just at different levels of generality. Once you have the central idea, a transport system with density-dependent flux will jam when the feedback between density and speed/growth is strong enough, each paper is filling in a different piece of the picture. The payoff from grinding through them is that you build a map of the terrain before you start coding.






NoteWhat I pulled from each paper



Datta, Delius & Law (2011) — Most important. Same equations, same institution. Derives the exact stability conditions for the McKendrick-von Foerster equation: large predator:prey ratio \(\beta\), small diet breadth \(\sigma\), low feeding efficiency \(K\) all push toward instability.
Rochet & Benoît (2012) — Most directly relevant biologically. Shows that selective fishing amplifies oscillations in the size spectrum, with large fish being far more destabilising targets than small fish. The phase portrait in (selectivity, intensity) space is essentially the diagram the project wants to produce.
Bando et al. (1995) — Clearest derivation of the instability condition: \(V'(b) > a/2\). Uniform traffic jams if the slope of the velocity function exceeds half the driver sensitivity. Maps directly onto the fish model.
Kerner & Konhäuser (1994) — Three-regime phase structure: stable, metastable, unstable. The metastable regime (where a large perturbation can nucleate a jam even though small ones die out) is likely to appear in MIZER too.



The Ranking
After skimming through all 20, the top 5 order of importance for this project is:

Datta, Delius & Law (2011)
Rochet & Benoît (2012)
Bando et al. (1995)
Kerner & Konhäuser (1994)
Sugiyama et al. (2008)

Papers 1 and 2 are in a different tier as they’re the core theoretical and biological foundation. Papers 3-5 build intuition.

What Tomorrow Looks Like
Tomorrow is about getting hands-on with MIZER. The goal is to build a single-species model feeding on a resource with a low replenishment rate, and start feeling out the parameter space. No polished results expected because this is an intuition-building session.
Concretely, that means:

Getting MIZER installed and running in R
Following the MIZER course fishing scenarios tutorial to understand the basic API
Building the simplest possible single-species model (one species, one resource)
Setting the resource replenishment rate \(r\) low and watching what happens to the size spectrum
Trying to reproduce something that looks like a jam — a localised excess of fish at one size class that self-amplifies rather than smoothing out

The aim isn’t to find the exact bifurcation point tomorrow but instead to confirm that the instability exists in MIZER at all and get a feel for which parameters matter most.

Reflection
Honestly, today was a good day. The literature is dense but it’s tractable, and the more you sit with the traffic analogy the more natural it feels. The fish model and the traffic model are not just metaphorically similar but structurally identical in the way that matters: both are conservation laws with density-dependent flux, and both jam when the feedback between density and transport rate is strong enough.
What the project adds is the simulation side, pushing the model into regimes the analytical approach can’t easily reach, and the intervention side by using fishing to actively reshape the dynamics rather than just observe them.
Plenty to get on with. On to the code.

title: Day 3: Contents Pages, Oscillations & the Power Law Realisation
text:
Afternoon: Hunting for Oscillations
With the blog in better shape, I got back to the main task: trying to produce interesting dynamics in the single species mizer model.
The question from Day 2 had been nagging at me. The previous attempts at perturbing the size spectrum, bumping up abundance in different size ranges, kept converging back to steady state without producing anything that looked like a genuine oscillation or instability. The spectrum would wobble briefly and then flatten out again. Convincing yourself you’ve found something when you’ve just produced a slightly delayed equilibrium is a trap worth avoiding.
Today it finally clicked and the fix was conceptually simple once I saw it.

The Key Insight: Resource Rate Is a Power Law
When I’d been “reducing the resource rate” in earlier experiments, I’d been setting it to a constant. That’s not a small reduction but changing the shape of the function, not just its magnitude. You end up with a resource that replenishes at the same rate regardless of size, which is biologically wrong and dynamically different.
The correct way to reduce the resource rate while keeping the physics intact is to scale the existing power law by multiplying the whole curve by a small scalar. This preserves the size-dependence while genuinely suppressing replenishment across the board:
p <- newSingleSpeciesParams(lambda = 2.05)

r <- resource_rate(p)       # extract the power law
r <- r * 0.0001             # scale it down uniformly
p <- setResource(p,
  resource_rate = r,
  resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat"
)
That single change, extracting the rate, scaling it, and putting it back, made all the difference.


Adding the Initial Perturbation
With the resource replenishment suppressed, I then bumped the initial fish abundance in the large size range (10–100 g) by a factor of 5:
rng <- c(10, 100)
idx <- p@w >= rng[1] & p@w <= rng[2]
initialN(p)[, idx] <- initialN(p)[, idx] * 5
This seeds a localised excess of fish at large body sizes which is exactly the kind of perturbation that should reveal whether the system has an oscillatory or damped response.


The Full Experiment

library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
# Build params
p <- newSingleSpeciesParams(lambda = 2.05)
# Deviation from power law
deviation_plot <- function(sim, title) {
  spec <- finalNResource(sim)
  expected <- p@w_full^(-2.05)
  deviation <- spec / expected
  plot(p@w_full, deviation, type = "l", log = "x",
       main = title, xlab = "Size (g)", ylab = "Deviation from power law")
  abline(h = 1, lty = 2)
}

# Scale down resource rate as a power law (not a constant)
r <- resource_rate(p)
r <- r * 0.0001
p <- setResource(p,
                 resource_rate = r,
                 resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat"
)

# Perturb the large size range
rng <- c(10, 100)
idx <- p@w >= rng[1] & p@w <= rng[2]
initialN(p)[, idx] <- initialN(p)[, idx] * 5

# Run simulation
sim <- project(p, t_max = 20, t_save = 0.5)







Note



Deviation Plot:
The reason why the deviation plot looks so small is due to the fact that this is being run when the population as almost gone back to the steady state.

# Deviation from power law
deviation_plot(sim, "Deviation — bump at large range")











animateSpectra(sim, resource = FALSE, log_x = FALSE, log_y = FALSE, power = 2)







The Result
Something genuinely interesting showed up. In the early part of the simulation, the spectrum doesn’t just relax but oscillates, with the abundance overshooting and undershooting before eventually settling. The fine time resolution (t_save = 0.5) was important here; a coarser save interval would have smoothed straight over it.
That said, the oscillation is transient. By the end of the run the system does converge back to steady state so this isn’t a self-sustaining instability, at least not under these parameters. What it is is a clear sign that the dynamics are richer than a pure monotonic decay: the system has enough inertia to ring before it settles.
That’s worth understanding better before drawing conclusions.

title: Day 3: Contents Pages, Oscillations & the Power Law Realisation
text:
What This Means
The Day 2 experiments weren’t wrong, they were just missing a critical detail. A resource rate reduced to a constant rather than scaled as a power law is a different model, not a lower-resource version of the same model. That distinction matters because mizer’s steady-state dynamics are calibrated around the power law structure: changing the shape breaks assumptions that the rest of the model depends on.
The lesson generalises: when you want to weaken a power law, multiply it but don’t replace it.
As for the transient oscillation, the next step is to understand what’s governing its decay. Is the system genuinely stable under these parameters, just with a slow ring-down? Or are there parameters we can change where the oscillation stops decaying and becomes self-sustaining? That’s the boundary worth finding.

text:

The answer required shifting from plotting biomass directly to plotting flux, the rate at which biomass flows through each size class.
Mizer provides getFlux() for exactly this, and most of the morning was spent getting to grips with what it returns and how best to display it.

title: Day 5: Visualising the Flux
text:
Setting Up
The same single-species setup as previous days: \(\lambda = 2.05\), \(\beta = 30\), \(\sigma = 0.5\), with a resource rate scaled down by a factor of 1000 and a fivefold perturbation applied to the large size class (10–100 g) in the initial condition.

library(mizer)

varying_beta_sigma_test <- function(beta_new = 100, sigma_new = 1.3) {
  test_sizes <- list(
    "small"  = c(0.1, 1),
    "medium" = c(1, 10),
    "large"  = c(10, 100)
  )
  p <- newSingleSpeciesParams(lambda = 2.05, beta = beta_new, sigma = sigma_new)

  r <- resource_rate(p)
  r <- r * 0.001
  p <- setResource(p, resource_rate = r, resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  rng <- test_sizes[["large"]]
  idx <- p@w >= rng[1] & p@w <= rng[2]
  initialN(p)[, idx] <- initialN(p)[, idx] * 5

  project(p, t_max = 100, t_save = 0.5)
}

sim <- varying_beta_sigma_test(30, 0.5)

title: Day 5: Visualising the Flux
text:
Exploring the Plots
The first plot was the energy growth rate across size classes over time:

plotHover(getEGrowth(sim))





This gives a sense of which sizes are gaining energy and how that changes over the simulation. But what was really of interest was the flux itself.

flux <- getFlux(sim)
plotHover(flux)





Raw flux is dominated by the smallest size classes, where numbers are enormous. To get a clearer picture of where the biomass is flowing rather than just the individuals, the flux can be weighted by body mass:

biomass_flux <- flux
biomass_flux[] <- sweep(flux, 3, w(getParams(sim)), "*")
plotHover(biomass_flux)





Finally, plotting both flux and biomass flux together on log-log axes lets you see the relationship between the two across the full size range:

plot2(biomass_flux, flux, log = "xy")

title: Day 5: Visualising the Flux
text:
What the Flux Plot Shows
The picture that emerged was stark. Flux is very high at the smallest sizes, around \(10^{-3}\) g, and drops sharply across several orders of magnitude, reaching essentially zero by 0.1 g. Very little biomass is successfully transiting into the larger size classes.
This is almost certainly a consequence of the extremely low resource rate. With so little food available, the growth rates at intermediate and large sizes are negligible, and the perturbation applied to the large size class has almost no pathway through which it can be replenished. The oscillations seen in previous days are playing out almost entirely in the small-to-medium size range.
It raises a question for later: what does the flux look like under a more realistic resource rate? Is the sharp cutoff a property of the model or an artefact of the deliberately depleted resource?

title: Day 5: Visualising the Flux
text:
Afternoon: Strogatz Chapter 5
The afternoon shifted to theory. Chapter 5 of Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos by Strogatz moves from one-dimensional flows to nonlinear flows in two dimensions, and the step up in richness is immediate.
In one dimension, a trajectory has nowhere to go but left or right. In two dimensions, the phase plane opens up and fixed points acquire character: stable and unstable nodes, saddle points, spirals, centres. Trajectories can approach a fixed point along a preferred direction, orbit around it indefinitely, or be repelled.
The analytical core of the chapter is linearisation. Near a fixed point, a nonlinear system can be approximated by a linear one, and the Jacobian evaluated at that point tells you everything about local behaviour. The eigenvalues of the Jacobian determine whether trajectories spiral in or out, approach along a curve, or diverge and a clean diagram classifying fixed points by the trace and determinant of the Jacobian puts the whole picture in one place.
What resonates most clearly with the simulation work is the limit of linearisation. It is precise and useful near a fixed point, but says nothing about the global structure of the phase plane: whether distant trajectories eventually converge, whether limit cycles exist, or whether the system can be pushed from one basin of attraction into another. That gap between local and global is exactly what made the flux plots this morning interesting. The model’s local behaviour near steady state is one thing, but following where the biomass actually goes is another.
The next chapter will presumably start closing that gap. For now, the foundations are solid.
